newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Yeltsin is changed man after illness.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Yeltsin is changed man after illness.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, a hugely changed man after months of illness, seems more in control than he has been in years and is acting like a different type of president.

His role and image appear to have changed. Yeltsin is leaving day-to-day affairs to his reformist government and behaving like a father figure, leading his country in a thoughtful, unconfrontational and consistent way.

Yeltsin, a born fighter, has always been at his best at times of crises and appeared to fade away when it came to routine work. There is no crisis now, but the 66-year-old leader remains on top of the job although his health at times still seems shaky.
A combination of factors seems to have brought about Yeltsin's transformation.
Yeltsin has no constitutional right to stand for a third term and may be thinking now more about his future place in history rather than short-term interests.

And there are no political foes to match him in Russia. The opposition-dominated State Duma or lower house of parliament has limited powers, and even the communists are reluctant to challenge Yeltsin head-on. An election is not due until 2000.
But first deputy speaker of the Duma Alexander Shokhin on Wednesday made public an idea which has been floating in the Kremlin for a long time.

Shokhin said that, if Russia and the former Soviet republic of Belarus merge into a single state, Yeltsin might have a legal opportunity to stand for its presidency. The two Slav neighbours have been moving since last year towards closer integration.

If such an election takes place, and if Yeltsin's health permits him to stand, he will need a positive record -- something he is earning now. The motto of fighting communism which helped him win his second term last year is unlikely to work again.
Up to this year, Yeltsin faced one crisis after another.

First elected in June 1991, he faced a coup attempt by Soviet hardliners the same year, then a protracted power struggle with the then powerful parliament. That culminated in bloodshed in 1993 when he sent tanks to shell the parliament building.

In 1994 Yeltsin sent troops to the breakaway region of Chechnya. The war, which killed tens of thousands there, stopped only last August, two months after he won a second term -- but overstrained his heart in the process.
He was out of action for most of the second half of the year and had a quintuple bypass operation in November.
Yeltsin's new image could be linked to his health. Doctors say a person's psychology may change after major heart surgery.
The Kremlin says the 66-year old leader has recovered from the operation and from a bout of pneumonia he suffered in January.
But he does not seem quite well, and concern about his health rose after an less-than-convincing physical performance in Germany last month.

Yeltsin takes frequent breaks from the Kremlin. Last month he went to his once-favourite Black Sea resort of Sochi. But he could not swim or play tennis -- his favourite pastimes -- and came back early. On Wednesday he went to a hunting lodge near Moscow.
But mentally and psychologically, Yeltsin is very much on top.
He proved it convincingly in a 30-minute television interview on Wednesday, which, filmed outdoors on a sunny, spring day, dealt with several major issues.

Yeltsin chose the day when a long and heated debate between Moscow and NATO over plans by the Western defence alliance to expand eastwards was resolved, and he praised the deal as a victory for Russia.

He grabbed the initiative from controversial and ambitious Belarussian leader Alexander Lukashenko on integration with Belarus by saying the Kremlin saw a single merged state in the future -- clearly with Russia playing the dominant role.

At the moment Russia's biggest problem is the economy and Yeltsin appears to realise that reformers in the government are better placed to tackle it if he provides a strong political cover, which he did on Wednesday.
He said he was happy with the new team of ministers who did not "let me doze off" and generated new ideas every day.
He felt strong enough to praise Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov, who had led the military resistance to the Russian troops, as "a clever man with great authority in Chechnya".
